title: LinkedIn Launches
summary: LinkedIn goes live as a professional networking site, creating the first major social network focused on careers and business connections.
narrative: Reid Hoffman launches LinkedIn with a simple idea: your professional network should be online. At first, it's just a digital Rolodex — you connect with people you know professionally. There's no news feed, no status updates, no photos. Just connections and resumes. Recruiters love it. Headhunters love it. Within a year, it has 1.6 million users. It's not sexy like Friendster or MySpace, but it's useful. LinkedIn proves that social networking isn't just for teenagers — it's for anyone who wants a job.
why_it_matters: Created the professional social network category. Changed how hiring works forever. Proved social networking had value beyond entertainment.

title: Mac OS X Jaguar Refines the Experience
summary: Apple releases Mac OS X 10.2 Jaguar, the first version that feels truly polished and starts converting Windows users.
narrative: Mac OS X 10.0 was buggy. 10.1 was better. But 10.2 Jaguar is where it clicks. Sherlock 3 does internet searching from the desktop. iChat integrates with AIM. Address Book syncs everything. The Finder gets a real search. Quartz Extreme accelerates graphics with the GPU. For the first time, Mac OS X feels like a complete, polished operating system. Windows users start taking notice. Apple's 'Switch' ad campaign begins. The Mac renaissance has started.
why_it_matters: First truly polished Mac OS X release. Validated Apple's transition from classic Mac OS. Made the Mac viable for mainstream users again.

title: Camera Phones Enter the Mainstream
summary: Japan's J-Phone launches the first camera phone with built-in sharing, while Samsung and others bring the technology to the US.
narrative: The Sharp J-SH04 launches in Japan in late 2000, but 2002 is when camera phones go global. Samsung, Nokia, and Ericsson release phones with cameras that can actually take decent photos. In Japan, 'Sha-mail' — picture messaging — becomes a cultural phenomenon. Americans are slower to adopt, but the trend is clear: everyone will have a camera in their pocket. It's 0.3 megapixels. It's terrible quality. It's the future.
why_it_matters: Put a camera in every pocket. Created the foundation for Instagram, Snapchat, and the entire visual social media economy. Changed how we document daily life.
image_caption: Japan's J-Phone launches the first camera phone with built-in sharing, while Samsung and others bring the technology to the US.

title: Microsoft Launches Tablet PC Edition
summary: Microsoft releases Windows XP Tablet PC Edition, an ambitious attempt to bring pen computing to the mainstream.
narrative: Bill Gates takes the stage and declares 'the tablet PC' the future of computing. He's got Fujitsu, Toshiba, and others building pen-input laptops that rotate and fold flat. You can write notes, draw diagrams, annotate documents. It's brilliant in theory. In practice, the hardware is heavy, the battery lasts two hours, and the handwriting recognition is unreliable. It costs $2,000+. The tablet PC fails in 2002. But the idea doesn't die. Eight years later, Apple proves the concept was right — it just needed the right execution.
why_it_matters: First mainstream tablet computing attempt. Proved the concept was viable but the execution wasn't ready. Laid groundwork for the iPad revolution.
image_caption: Microsoft releases Windows XP Tablet PC Edition, an ambitious attempt to bring pen computing to the mainstream.

title: Xbox Live Launches Online Gaming
summary: Microsoft launches Xbox Live, the first major unified online gaming service for consoles, pioneering voice chat and online multiplayer.
narrative: Microsoft does something bold: every Xbox comes with a broadband adapter. You buy a $50 annual subscription, create a Gamertag, and you're online. Voice chat. Friends lists. Matchmaking. Halo 2 is still two years away, but the infrastructure is being built now. Sony has online features too, but they're fragmented. Xbox Live is unified, consistent, and it just works. The voice chat alone is revolutionary — you can trash-talk opponents in real time. It's the foundation of modern console gaming.
why_it_matters: Pioneered unified console online services. Voice chat changed gaming culture. Created the Gamertag identity system. Set the standard for Xbox Live and PlayStation Network.
image_caption: Microsoft launches Xbox Live, the first major unified online gaming service for consoles, pioneering voice chat and online multiplayer.

title: Wi-Fi Standard Gains Momentum
summary: The 802.11b Wi-Fi standard becomes widely adopted, and the faster 802.11a and 802.11g standards emerge.
narrative: In 2002, 'Wi-Fi' enters the mainstream vocabulary. Apple's AirPort has been around since 1999, but now every coffee shop, hotel, and airport wants to offer wireless internet. Intel launches the Centrino platform, bundling Wi-Fi with laptops. The 802.11b standard offers 11 Mbps — fast enough for web browsing and email. The new 802.11g standard pushes to 54 Mbps. Suddenly, wires feel outdated. The couch becomes a workstation. The kitchen table becomes an office. Freedom from the Ethernet cable changes everything.
why_it_matters: Freed computing from Ethernet cables. Enabled the mobile computing revolution. Made coffee shops the new offices. Prerequisite for smartphones, tablets, and IoT.
image_caption: The 802.11b Wi-Fi standard becomes widely adopted, and the faster 802.11a and 802.11g standards emerge.

title: Blogging Reaches the Mainstream
summary: Blogging platforms like Blogger and LiveJournal explode in popularity, turning everyday people into publishers.
narrative: Google acquires Blogger in 2003, but the groundwork is laid in 2002. LiveJournal and Blogger make it possible for anyone to publish their thoughts to the world. Political bloggers like Andrew Sullivan and the Drudge Report influence elections. Tech bloggers cover Silicon Valley like beat reporters. Personal bloggers write about their lives, their diets, their breakups. The media establishment is terrified. 'Anyone can be a journalist' is both the promise and the threat. The blog is the first true social media format.
why_it_matters: Democratized publishing. Created the citizen journalism movement. Changed how news is reported and consumed. The ancestor of Twitter, Medium, and Substack.
image_caption: Blogging platforms like Blogger and LiveJournal explode in popularity, turning everyday people into publishers.

title: Enron Collapse Exposes Corporate Fraud
summary: Enron's spectacular collapse reveals massive accounting fraud and shatters trust in corporate America and the internet economy.
narrative: Enron was the darling of the dot-com era — a 'new economy' company that traded energy like a tech stock. Its stock hit $90 in August 2000. By October 2002, it's worth $0.60. Arthur Andersen, one of the Big Five accounting firms, goes down with it. 20,000 employees lose their jobs and retirement savings. Congress passes the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The scandal makes people skeptical of corporate promises, especially 'new economy' ones. The hangover from the dot-com bubble just got worse.
why_it_matters: Largest corporate fraud in history at the time. Led to Sarbanes-Oxley regulation. Shattered trust in corporate accounting and the 'new economy' narrative.
image_caption: Enron's spectacular collapse reveals massive accounting fraud and shatters trust in corporate America and the internet economy.

title: Juicy Couture Velour & Avril Lavigne's Pop-Punk Skater Look
summary: Paris Hilton made pink velour Juicy tracksuits ubiquitous, while 17-year-old Avril Lavigne led a pop-punk revolution.
narrative: Street fashion splintered in 2002: paparazzi photos showed Paris Hilton and Kim Kardashian living in matching pastel Juicy Couture velour tracksuits with 'JUICY' emblazoned across the back. Meanwhile, 17-year-old Canadian singer Avril Lavigne dropped 'Let Go', pairing loose men's neckties over white tank tops, baggy skater shorts, and studded wristbands in her 'Sk8er Boi' video, sparking a wave of mall-punk style.
why_it_matters: The contrasting aesthetics showed how teen culture was negotiating between ultra-glam consumerism and alternative rebellion.

title: American Idol Debuts & Kelly Clarkson Crowned
summary: Fox launched American Idol, turning Simon Cowell's scathing critique and audience landline voting into a national ritual.
narrative: Over 22 million viewers tuned into the live finale as Texas cocktail waitress Kelly Clarkson belted out 'A Moment Like This', tears streaming down her face. Simon Cowell's blunt British takedowns and Ryan Seacrest's countdowns gripped living rooms. Viewers flooded phone lines with over 15 million votes, demonstrating the power of interactive mass entertainment.
why_it_matters: American Idol dominated American television ratings for eight consecutive years and created the prototype for reality competition television.
image_caption: Fox launched American Idol, turning Simon Cowell's scathing critique and audience landline voting into a national ritual.

title: Eminem Drops 'Lose Yourself' & Conquers Hollywood in '8 Mile'
summary: Eminem's semi-autobiographical film 8 Mile became a box office smash, and 'Lose Yourself' won the Academy Award.
narrative: Opening with 'his palms are sweaty, knees weak, arms are heavy, mom's spaghetti', 'Lose Yourself' became one of hip-hop's most indelible anthems. The film '8 Mile', directed by Curtis Hanson, grossed $242 million and earned critical acclaim for capturing Detroit battle rap culture. When 'Lose Yourself' won the Oscar for Best Original Song, Eminem was asleep at home, having assumed a rap song had zero chance of winning.
why_it_matters: It was the first hip-hop song in history to win an Academy Award, establishing rap's artistic credibility among traditional cultural institutions.
image_caption: Eminem's semi-autobiographical film 8 Mile became a box office smash, and 'Lose Yourself' won the Academy Award.
